newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. expert makes case for boosting population aid.
newsitem.headline: U.N. expert makes case for boosting population aid.

text.p: A population expert on Tuesday predicted a sharp rise in abortions and infant and maternal deaths in poor countries if aid for reproductive-health programmes continues to stagnate.

Nafis Sadik, executive director of the U.N. Population Fund, estimated there would be at least 120 million additional unwanted pregnancies, 49 million more abortions, 5 million more deaths of infants and young children, and 65,000 more maternal deaths by 2000 unless aid grew.
The United States, once a leader with $580 million in assistance, now provides only $375 million because of a general decrease in foreign aid and a domestic debate over abortion.
"The fact we provide family planning information and services as opposed to abortion information and services -- that distinction is not always understood," Sadik told a news conference.
"We want to reduce the dependence on abortion, and the best way to do that is to increase access to information and services about contraceptives," she said.

Sadik, a Pakistani physician, said contributions after the 1994 Cairo population conference, which she ran, increased by 40 percent but then leveled off in 1996-7 despite pledges countries made to earmark $17 billion annually for reproductive health and family planning.
Two-thirds of these costs were to be met by developing countries themselves and one-third, or $5.7 billion, by rich nations, either through U.N. agencies or other assistance.

Developing countries and some in eastern Europe seem to be on track, having spent about $7.5 billion on population programmes in 1995. But aid from industrial countries, which jumped to $2 billion in 1995, did not continue to rise.
France, Italy and Belgium have also slacked off in assistance, while Britain, Norway, Denmark and the Netherlands have been strong donors.

The U.N. Population Fund has programmes in 140 countries but targets 60 of the poorest nations. Data Sadik presented showed that the unmet need for contraceptives among married couples ranged from 14 percent of couples in Brazil, Colombia, Indonesia and Sri Lanka to 25 percent in Bolivia, Ghana, Kenya and Togo.
Some programmes, Sadik said, have begun in Russia and Ukraine, where abortion is the main method of contraception.
